items.title: A Composable AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for 3D-IC Thermal Modeling
items.summary: Accurate thermal analysis of heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC packages is essential yet computationally prohibitive. A single full-package FEM simulation can take hours, while AI-based surrogates treat the entire stack as a monolithic prediction target and must be retrained whenever the die count or topology changes. To address this limitation, this work proposes Domain-Decomposed AI-Accelerated Iterative Solver for Thermal Analysis (DAIST), a composable thermal solver that decomposes the global package simulation into block-level subdomain problems, replaces subdomain solvers with neural operators, and couples them through iterative exchanges of interfacial temperature and heat flux. This local-to-global architecture eliminates the topology lock-in of monolithic models: block-level neural operators can be directly reused in unseen package assemblies without retraining. The iterative coupling strategy further provides a controllable accuracy-runtime tradeoff, where the iteration budget can be adjusted to trade accuracy for runtime. Evaluated on a multi-chiplet system and an advanced packaging system, DAIST achieves up to $178\times$ speedup over traditional FEM solvers with mean temperature errors of 0.068% and 0.323%, respectively, while demonstrating cross-topology reuse of block-level models across structurally distinct package assemblies.

items.title: Beyond principlism: Practical strategies for ethical AI use in research practices
items.summary: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research, particularly large language models (LLMs), has outpaced the development of ethical guidelines, leading to a "Triple-Too" problem: too many high-level ethical initiatives, too abstract principles lacking contextual and practical relevance, and too much focus on restrictions and risks over benefits and utilities. Existing approaches--principlism (reliance on abstract ethical principles), formalism (rigid application of rules), and technological solutionism (overemphasis on technological fixes)--offer little practical guidance for addressing ethical challenges of AI in scientific research practices. To bridge the gap between abstract principles and day-to-day research practices, a user-centered, realism-inspired approach is proposed here. It outlines five specific goals for ethical AI use: 1) understanding model training and output, including bias mitigation strategies; 2) respecting privacy, confidentiality, and copyright; 3) avoiding plagiarism and policy violations; 4) applying AI beneficially compared to alternatives; and 5) using AI transparently and reproducibly. Each goal is accompanied by actionable strategies and realistic cases of misuse and corrective measures. I argue that ethical AI application requires evaluating its utility against existing alternatives rather than isolated performance metrics. Additionally, I propose documentation guidelines to enhance transparency and reproducibility in AI-assisted research. Moving forward, we need targeted professional development, training programs, and balanced enforcement mechanisms to promote responsible AI use while fostering innovation. By refining these ethical guidelines and adapting them to emerging AI capabilities, we can accelerate scientific progress without compromising research integrity.

items.title: Prefill/Decode-Aware Evaluation of LLM Inference on Emerging AI Accelerators
items.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in latency- and cost-sensitive settings, inference efficiency has become a central systems challenge. While GPUs dominate current deployments, a growing number of AI accelerators claim advantages for LLM inference, yet it remains unclear under which conditions such accelerators outperform GPUs in practice. Recent inference systems decompose execution into Prefill and Decode phases, which exhibit distinct computational characteristics and latency metrics, commonly captured by time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT). This paper presents a phase-aware evaluation of LLM inference performance across GPUs and emerging AI accelerators using a common model, Llama2-7B. By separately measuring Prefill and Decode performance, we reveal that accelerator advantages differ by phase and metric. Our results show that GPUs consistently excel in the compute-intensive Prefill phase, while GroqRack achieves significantly lower TPOT during Decode (batching not currently supported). However, GPUs regain an advantage in Decode throughput as batch size increases. These findings demonstrate that each platform exhibits distinct phase-dependent strengths. We further analyze heterogeneous Prefill/Decode disaggregation across different accelerator platforms, identifying performance gains and the workload and network conditions under which such gains are realized.

items.title: The Pitfall of Evaluating Performance on Emerging AI Accelerators
items.summary: In recent years, domain-specific hardware has brought significant performance improvements in deep learning (DL). Both industry and academia only focus on throughput when evaluating these AI accelerators, which usually are custom ASICs deployed in datacenter to speed up the inference phase of DL workloads. Pursuing higher hardware throughput such as OPS (Operation Per Second) using various optimizations seems to be their main design target. However, they ignore the importance of accuracy in the DL nature. Motivated by this, this paper argue that a single throughput metric can not comprehensively reflect the real-world performance of AI accelerators. To reveal this pitfall, we evaluates several frequently-used optimizations on a typical AI accelerator and quantifies their impact on accuracy and throughout under representative DL inference workloads. Based on our experimental results, we find that some optimizations cause significant loss on accuracy in some workloads, although it can improves the throughout. Furthermore, our results show the importance of end-to-end evaluation in DL.

items.title: Boolean Matrix Logic Programming on the GPU
items.summary: Traditional logic programming relies on symbolic computation on the CPU, which can limit performance for large-scale inference tasks. Recent advances in GPU hardware enable high-throughput matrix operations, motivating a shift toward parallel logic inference. Boolean Matrix Logic Programming (BMLP) introduces a novel approach to datalog query evaluation using Boolean matrix algebra, well-suited to GPU acceleration. Building on this paradigm, we present two GPU-accelerated BMLP algorithms for bottom-up inference over linear dyadic recursive datalog programs. We further extend the BMLP theoretical framework to support general linear recursion with binary predicates. Empirical evaluations on reachability queries in large directed graphs and the Freebase 15K dataset show that our methods achieve 1-4 orders of magnitude speed up over state-of-the-art systems. These results demonstrate that Boolean matrix-based reasoning can significantly advance the scalability and efficiency of logic programming on modern hardware. Source code is available on https://github.com/lun-ai/BMLP.git.

# AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president

Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.

Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released. But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."

Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology is a threat to humanity. [...] The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this.

He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way.

items.summary:
𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗨𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗢𝘄𝗻 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮?

Meet Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — a powerful architecture that connects Large Language Models (LLMs) with external knowledge sources.

Instead of relying only on pre-trained knowledge, RAG retrieves relevant information from your data before generating an answer.

𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗮 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 👇

𝟭. 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Gather information from PDFs, websites, databases, documents, and other knowledge sources.

𝟮. 𝗧𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗦𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴

Break large documents into smaller sections so the system can search and retrieve information more efficiently.

𝟯. 𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗘𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀

Transform text chunks into numerical vectors that represent their semantic meaning.

𝟰. 𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝘅𝗶𝗻𝗴

Store vectors, original text, and metadata in a searchable vector database.

𝟱. 𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹

Convert the user's question into a vector and find the most relevant information from the knowledge base.

𝟲. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴

Combine the retrieved information with the original query to provide useful context to the LLM.

𝟳. 𝗔𝗜 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲

The LLM uses the supplied context to generate a relevant and informative response.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗥𝗔𝗚 𝗧𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗡𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹?

Modern RAG systems use advanced techniques to improve performance:

→ Hybrid Search
→ Reranking
→ Query Rewriting
→ Metadata Filtering
→ Context Compression
→ RAG Evaluation
→ Agentic RAG

𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿

RAG doesn't change what an LLM learned during training. It gives the model access to relevant external information when answering questions.

The quality of a RAG application ultimately depends on how effectively it retrieves, organizes, and uses information.

Better Retrieval = Better Context = More Useful AI Responses.

Which concept should we explore next: Vector Databases, Embeddings, Hybrid Search, or Agentic RAG?

items.title: Qwen3.8-27B reportedly reached 381 tokens per second on a single RTX 3090 with 24GB VRAM
items.summary:
Qwen3.8-27B reportedly reached 381 tokens per second on a single RTX 3090 with 24GB VRAM

The original setup was running at approximately 82 tok/s. After several inference optimisations, the developer pushed throughput to roughly 4.6 times the starting speed without changing the GPU

Here is how the performance evolved:

•Initial setup: ~82 tok/s
•Optimised MTP: ~114 tok/s
•DFlash2 + context lookup: ~138 tok/s
•Optimised lookup verification: ~381 tok/s

The biggest improvement came from changing how the system handles text that already exists in the input context

1. DFlash2 reduces sequential token generation

Autoregressive models generate text one token at a time. Each new token depends on the previous output, creating a sequential bottleneck

Speculative decoding addresses this by allowing a smaller draft mechanism to propose multiple tokens ahead.

The main model then verifies those proposals. When they are accepted, the system can generate several tokens without performing the usual sequence of individual decoding steps

DFlash2 uses this approach to reduce the amount of sequential work required during generation

2. Context lookup takes advantage of existing text

The developer added context lookup, which searches the input prompt for sequences that may match the model’s expected output

Consider a model processing a 25K-token document

If it needs to reproduce a paragraph, code block or other passage from that document, generating every token from scratch is unnecessary work

Context lookup can find matching text, propose it as a sequence of candidate tokens, and let the main model verify it

The optimised implementation reportedly increased verification blocks from seven tokens to as many as 16

The developer also reports that approximately 15 out of 16 proposed tokens were accepted per verification step in the tested workload

That high acceptance rate is important. Speculative decoding only saves substantial time when the main model accepts most of the proposed tokens

With fewer rejected proposals and fewer sequential decoding steps, throughput increases considerably

3. Why the workload changes the result

On a document-reproduction task involving approximately 25K tokens, the reported performance was:

•Previous DFlash2 setup: ~260 tok/s
• Optimised context lookup: ~382 tok/s

This is where the 381 tok/s headline comes from

It is important not to confuse this with ordinary conversational generation speed

For general chat workloads, the developer reports approximately 133 tok/s

Context lookup works particularly well when generated output overlaps heavily with material already present in the prompt. It won’t produce the same gains when the model is writing original content, solving unfamiliar problems or generating text with little overlap with its input

Potential applications include document processing, retrieval-augmented generation, code transformations and other tasks involving substantial reuse of existing text

4. Prefix caching makes repeated questions much faster

There is another optimisation in the setup: prefix caching

When you ask a second question about the same 25K-token document, the shared prompt prefix does not necessarily need to be processed again from scratch

The inference engine can reuse previously computed prefix information and process the new portion of the request

In the developer’s reported test, time to first token dropped from 22.4 seconds to 0.56 seconds

That’s roughly a 40× reduction in time to first token for the repeated-document scenario

The model still needs to process the new question and generate an answer. The saving comes from avoiding redundant computation on the shared prefix

The bigger picture

This result shows why local inference performance cannot be judged by GPU specifications alone

The same RTX 3090 and the same Qwen3.8-27B model can deliver very different performance depending on how the inference engine handles generation https://t.co/AlxGxC0hoI

items.title: By  @AI_TechSparks
items.summary:
By  @AI_TechSparks
Beyond Flat Vector Search: The Real Architecture and ROI of GraphRAG

Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is hitting a structural ceiling in enterprise environments. Simple vector similarity searches are excellent for fetching isolated facts, but they completely fail when an executive asks: "Give me a high-level summary of our entire Q3 procurement risks."

To extract holistic insights across disconnected corporate data silos, Silicon Valley is shifting toward GraphRAG.

By combining traditional vector indexing with a Knowledge Graph structure, GraphRAG maps not just chunks of text, but the explicit semantic relationships between entities (companies, themes, deployment logs, metrics).

However, before you overhaul your data infrastructure, you must understand the real architectural trade-offs and token costs:

The Indexing Penalty: Building a GraphRAG pipeline is intensely resource-heavy. During the ingestion phase, you cannot just generate fast vector embeddings. You must run every document through an LLM to extract entity-relationship triplets. For a corpus of 10,000 enterprise PDFs, this extraction layer can spike your upfront token costs by 10x to 50x compared to traditional indexing.

Global vs. Local Query Routing: GraphRAG changes how agents access data. For targeted technical lookups, "Local Search" queries specific graph neighborhoods, delivering hyper-precise context at a low cost. For strategic, cross-departmental questions, "Global Search" scans pre-generated community summaries across the entire graph. This provides unprecedented synthesis but results in massive context window consumption per query.
The Decoupled Stack Reality: True enterprise GraphRAG requires tight orchestration between a reliable graph store (Neo4j, AWS Neptune) and a high-performance vector database (Pinecone, Qdrant). If your team tries to build this natively inside a single monolithic framework without isolating the graph queries from the inference layer, latency will degrade dramatically under enterprise production workloads.
The takeaway for CTOs: GraphRAG is not a drop-in replacement for standard vector search. It is an advanced semantic layer. Deploy it only where your autonomous agents genuinely require cross-document synthesis and relationship mapping. For standard, single-document retrieval, keep your pipeline lean and deterministic.

Are your engineering teams auditing the real token ROI of your current RAG infrastructure?

1. DFlash2 reduces sequential decoding

Autoregressive models generate text one token at a time.

The main model then verifies those proposals. When the proposed tokens are accepted, the engine can advance through multiple tokens without performing the usual sequence of individual decoding steps.

However, speculative decoding is only effective when the draft proposals are accepted frequently enough. Rejected tokens require additional work and reduce the potential speedup.

Imagine asking Qwen3.8-27B to process a 25K-token document and reproduce a particular paragraph or code block.

Without context lookup, the model has to generate that passage token by token, even though the exact text already exists in its input.

Context lookup searches the existing prompt for sequences that could match the model’s expected output.

It can then propose those sequences as candidate tokens for the main model to verify.

Instead of generating every token from scratch, the engine attempts to reuse text that is already available.

The developer’s optimised implementation reportedly increased verification blocks from seven tokens to as many as 16.

More importantly, approximately 15 out of every 16 proposed tokens were accepted in the tested workload.

That’s an acceptance rate of roughly 94%.

A high acceptance rate means the system spends less time discarding incorrect proposals and more time advancing through accepted tokens.

This explains why the verification optimisation produced such a substantial improvement.

3. Why the workload makes such a difference

The 381 tokens/s result comes from a document-reproduction workload involving approximately 25K tokens.

The reported comparison was:

Previous DFlash2 configuration: ~260 tokens/s
Optimised context lookup: ~382 tokens/s

The developer also reports approximately 133 tokens/s for ordinary conversational generation.

That distinction is important.

Context lookup works particularly well when the model’s output overlaps heavily with material already present in its prompt.

It can be useful for:

Reproducing passages from long documents.
Code transformations involving existing source files.
Document processing.
Retrieval-augmented generation.
Tasks that require copying or restructuring existing text.

But it won’t produce the same gains when the model is generating original content, solving unfamiliar problems or producing responses with little overlap with the input.

The 381 tokens/s figure should therefore be treated as workload-specific, not as the model’s general chat speed.

4. Prefix caching dramatically reduces repeated prompt processing

There’s another optimisation in the setup: prefix caching.

items.title: The Evaluation Framework: The Most Underbuilt Part Of An AI System
items.summary:
# The Evaluation Framework: The Most Underbuilt Part Of An AI System

ByHiren Dhaduk,

Forbes Councils Member.

Hiren is CTO & co-founder of Simform, an AI-native digital engineering services company.

When a production AI system starts to lose quality, spotting the decline is only part of the problem. The harder question is whether the team can explain what changed and judge, with enough confidence, whether the next fix will actually improve the system. [...] A production evaluation framework has three parts: a maintained set of representative examples, a defined way to judge how the system performs on them and clear thresholds for deciding whether a change is ready to release. Together, they answer a practical question: What evidence is enough to say that the next version is better?

### The first part is the evaluation set: the examples the system will be tested against. [...] It may begin with historical or curated examples, but it should incorporate real production interactions, known failure patterns and situations the team did not anticipate before launch. When a meaningful production failure occurs, that case should become part of the evaluation set so future versions have to prove they do not recreate it.
